title: may and might 2
subtitle: I might go / We might as well walk
summary: Use may and might for possible future actions, choose might when the situation is not real, and use might as well when there is no better alternative.

lesson.heading: Possible actions in the future
lesson.text: We use **may** and **might** to talk about possible actions or happenings in the future (= perhaps it will happen). The negative forms are **may not** and **might not** (mightn't).

examples.text: I haven't decided where to go on holiday. I **may go** to Ireland.
Take an umbrella with you. It **might rain** later.
The bus isn't always on time. We **might have to wait** a few minutes.
examples.note: = perhaps we will have to wait

examples.text: Amy **may not go** out tonight. She isn't feeling well.
examples.note: = perhaps she will not go out

examples.text: There **might not be** enough time to discuss everything at the meeting.

lesson.heading: For sure or possible?

left.label: going to = for sure
examples: I'm going to buy a car.

right.label: may / might = possible
examples: I **may buy** a car. or I **might buy** a car.
I **might be going** (or I **may be going**) to Ireland soon.

lesson.note: We also use may/might be -ing for possible plans.

lesson.heading: may or might?
lesson.text: Usually you can use may or might. But we use **might** (not may) when the situation is not real. In *If they paid me better*, the situation is not real: they do not pay me well, so I'm not going to work harder.

examples.text: I **may go** to Ireland. or I **might go** to Ireland.
Jane **might be able to** help you. or Jane **may be able to** help you.
If they paid me better, I **might work** harder.

lesson.heading: will be -ing or may / might be -ing?

left.label: will be -ing = sure
examples: Don't phone at 8.30. I**'ll be watching** the football on TV.

right.label: might be -ing = perhaps
examples: Don't phone at 8.30. I **might be watching** the football on TV. (= perhaps I'll be watching it)

lesson.heading: might as well
lesson.text: Helen and Clare have just missed the bus. The buses run every hour. *What shall we do? Shall we walk?* - *We **might as well**. It's a nice day and I don't want to wait here for an hour.* **We might as well do something** = we should do it because there is no better alternative. There is no reason not to do it. You can also use **may as well**.

examples.text: *A:* What time are you going out? *B:* Well, I'm ready, so I **might as well go** now. or ... I **may as well go** now.
Buses are so expensive these days, you **might as well get** a taxi.
examples.note: = taxis are as good, no more expensive than buses

lesson.text: Decided = I'm going to ...; not decided = I might ... . And after an unreal if (If they paid me better ...), only might is possible.

exercises.prompt: A: Have you decided what sort of car you want to buy? B: Yes, ___ a sports car.
exercises.explanation: B has decided, so it is for sure: I'm going to get. Might is for something possible, not decided.

exercises.prompt: A: When is Tom coming to see us? B: He hasn't said yet. ___ on Sunday.
exercises.explanation: Nothing is decided, so it is only possible: He might come (might + infinitive without to).

exercises.prompt: A: Do you have plans for the weekend? B: Nothing fixed. ___.
exercises.explanation: Nothing fixed = not decided, so: I might go away.

exercises.prompt: Don't make too much noise. You ___ the baby.
exercises.explanation: A possible future happening: might wake (= perhaps you will wake the baby).

exercises.prompt: Be careful. This footpath is icy. You ___.
exercises.explanation: Perhaps you will slip: might + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase completes each sentence: might be able to or might have to?

items.text: Tell me about your problem. I ___ help you.
I can come to the meeting, but I ___ leave before the end.
I'm not free this evening, but I ___ meet you tomorrow evening.
I'm not sure whether this car park is free or not. We ___ pay.
There's a long queue. We ___ wait a long time.
'I've got a problem with my bike.' 'Let me have a look. I ___ fix it.'

exercises.prompt: I haven't seen him for a long time. I don't know if I will recognise him or not. Make a sentence with might not.
exercises.explanation: Perhaps I will not recognise him: might not + infinitive.

exercises.prompt: I've been invited to the wedding, but I'm not sure that I'll be able to go. Make a sentence with might not.
exercises.answer: I might not be able to go to the wedding.
exercises.explanation: Perhaps I won't be able to go: might not be able to.

exercises.statement: If they paid me better, I may work harder.
exercises.explanation: If they paid me better, I might work harder. The situation is not real (they don't pay me well), so we use might, not may.

exercises.statement: Don't phone at 8.30. I might be watching the football on TV.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Might be -ing = perhaps I'll be watching it at that time.

exercises.prompt: Your computer doesn't work any more and it will cost a lot to repair. You say: It's not worth repairing. I ___ a new one.
exercises.explanation: There is no better alternative, so: might as well buy.

exercises.prompt: You and a friend are at home and bored. There's a film on TV starting in a few minutes. You say: We ___ it. There's nothing else to do.
exercises.explanation: There is no reason not to watch it: might as well watch.
